newsitem.title: USA: Problems fewer for cosmetic breast implants.
newsitem.headline: Problems fewer for cosmetic breast implants.

text.p: Roughly one of every four women with a breast implant needs a second operation because of complications but those who got the implants for cosmetic reasons had the lowest rates of problems, a study has found.
Patients whose implants were put in after surgery to remove or prevent cancer were nearly three times more likely to develop a complication, doctors found.

The study, published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine, comes from the same team that reported in 1994 that breast implants did not increase the risk of connective tissue disease or immune system problems.
Officials at Dow Corning Corp., which was pushed into bankruptcy court in 1995 by breast implant litigation, said they were pleased by the findings.
"The study provides more evidence that the concern over breast implants is overblown," said Patti Klein, a staff epidemiologist with Dow Corning.
"Breast implants do not cause systemic disease as alleged, and while there are some local complications, they can be taken care of."
Dow Corning was the world's largest maker of silicone-gel breast implants before the U.S. Food and Drug Administration imposed a moratorium on them in 1992.
In its proposed plan of reorganization, the silicone joint venture between Dow Chemical Co. and Corning Inc has pledged $600 million to pay certain claims of women with implants.

Yet even among investigators who do not think that silicone implants can cause illness, "there is concern that local complications may be an important problem," the team led by Dr. Sherine Gabriel of the Mayo Clinic said.

To get a sense of how often those problems occur, the Gabriel group evaluated the cases of 749 Minnesota women who had implants between 1964 and 1991. They discovered that 23.8 percent ultimately developed some type of complication, usually within the first six months or so after the operation.
The most common problem was capsular contracture, where a sheath of collagen hardens around the implant. It occurred in 17.5 percent of the women.

The silicone or salt solution ruptured in at least one of the implanted breasts in 5.7 percent of the women, making that problem just as common as hematomas, which are caused when a blood vessel breaks and the blood accumulates and clots.
A wound infection or a collection of fluid at the wound site affected fewer than 2.6 percent of the women. Other complications were seen in fewer than 2 percent.
"The risk of complications was highest during the first few months after the insertion of the implant," the team said.

Half of all problems surfaced within the first year, often within the first two months after the implantation surgery. After that two-month period the risk of a problem leveled out a bit in the women whose implants were for cosmetic reasons.

Women getting implants after surgery to prevent or treat cancer had a complication rate three times higher. By the fifth anniversary of their implant, about one third had needed surgery to deal with some kind of problem.

When they looked at individual implants instead of individual women, the Gabriel team said 3.9 percent of the implants ruptured and leakage occurred in 1 percent, a rate much lower than in other studies. They also found a rate of just 17.5 percent for capsule contracture, lower than in another study where the rate was 37.6 percent.

The research group said the statistics did not take into consideration a woman's overall satisfaction with her implant. "Such data would add an important perspective to discussions about the proper role of breast implantation," they said.
